title: The Reference Lab · Interactive Codebase Onboarding

modules.title: The System, On One Screen
modules.summary: The product turns a static TypeScript config into a multi-stage KYB/credit application that external participants fill in, while AI enriches company data, walks ownership trees, and validates documents. This map is the whole product — click any box to see what it does. Each module below teaches one subsystem: interactive playgrounds respond to your changes, walkthrough panels step through actual source line by line, and checkpoints ask you to predict behaviour before moving on; your score persists in this browser.

nodes.label: Participant wizard
nodes.description: The React wizard external participants fill in. It holds application state in context + hooks and PATCHes deltas to the API — no Redux.

nodes.label: Rule engine (mirror)
nodes.description: The identical pure evaluator runs in the browser on every keystroke — same code as the server, so client and server can never disagree about what the form looks like.

nodes.label: Doc upload → S3
nodes.description: Documents go straight to S3 with a presigned PUT; the AI validation pipeline streams progress back to the card over SSE.

nodes.label: API routes
nodes.description: Three kinds of caller, three auth methods: analysts on sessions, participants on link + JWT, partner systems on bearer keys.

nodes.label: application-service
nodes.description: The transactional spine (~2,800 lines): every create, update, upload, submit, and decision passes through it — lock → guard → merge → recompute → commit → notify.

nodes.label: ClientConfig
nodes.description: A client's entire application as one static config object: fields composed from reusable field-sets, rules, computed values, and a people policy.

nodes.label: Postgres · JSONB
nodes.description: One JSONB blob per application in the applications.data column — every answer, person, document, and ownership edge.

nodes.label: Ownership engine
nodes.description: Walks registry ownership trees to find UBOs: credit-bounded exploration, cumulative per-identity math, honest unknowns. Nearly every recent PR is ENG-250.

nodes.label: AI doc validation
nodes.description: OCR → classify → clarity → adequacy → date rules → verdict. Deterministic code brackets the LLM at both ends.

nodes.label: Webhooks · Slack
nodes.description: Outbound events, QStash-queued and HMAC-signed, always fired after commit — a slow customer endpoint can never block a submit.

widgets.title: Why one JSONB blob?
widgets.body: A KYB form's shape is entirely config-driven and varies per client — a relational schema would need a migration for every new field. Storing answers as JSON lets one table serve every config. The trade-off: no SQL-level querying of answers, so the rule engine queries it in memory instead.

description.body: Just uploaded and confirmed into S3 + the JSONB. If the field has no validator configured, it skips straight to accepted with acceptanceReason "no_validator_configured". Otherwise the wizard opens the SSE validation stream.
The AI pipeline is running (see the Document Validation module): OCR → classify → clarity → adequacy → date rules. Progress streams to the card's ring at 10% / 50% / 75% / 90%.
✓ counts as complete. Reached by validation passing (acceptanceReason "validation_passed"), by having no validator, or by the participant accepting a soft-fail.
Passed with doubts (soft fail): moderate confidence, unexpected doc type, or missing fields. The participant can accept anyway or retry.
A hard validation fail (unknown doc type, critical clarity, name mismatch, confidence < 0.5). The participant must re-upload; each re-upload restarts at pending.
✓ counts as complete. A human override: the participant/compliance accepted despite a failure, recording a userOverrideReason for the audit trail.
✓ counts as complete. The participant skipped collection where rules allow, with a recorded reason.

commentary.body: Validation passed: the document is stamped accepted with acceptanceReason "validation_passed", and extracted identity fields auto-populate the person record.
Each re-upload restarts the machine at pending — there is no shortcut around validation.

widgets.title: The rule that matters
widgets.body: Completeness only counts a document done when it's accepted, forced, or skipped. Everything else blocks submit.

code: confidence?: number;    // 0-1, only for AI sources

caption.body: Provenance: every value knows where it came from. For each value in fields, a parallel entry in fieldMeta records its source — this powers the trust badges in the UI and decides what an analyst double-checks.

widgets.title: Gotcha you will hit in week one
widgets.body: Registry-supplied people and ownership rows are never hard-deleted by participants — "removing" one flips its source to registry_dismissed (a soft-delete that preserves the audit trail). That's why getActivePeople() / getActiveOwnership() wrap data.people / data.ownership everywhere. Forget the wrapper and dismissed rows reappear.

questions.prompt: A participant clicks "remove" on a director that came from the company registry. What happens to that Person row?

options.label: It is deleted from the people array
Its source flips to registry_dismissed — the row stays in the JSONB for the audit trail and is filtered out by getActivePeople()
Its confirmed flag is set to false
It is moved into the entities array

explanation.body: Registry-supplied rows are soft-deleted. Regulators care why a registry-supplied person disappeared, so the row survives with a dismissed source, an activity-log entry is written, and every consumer filters through getActivePeople().

questions.prompt: Which document statuses count as "complete" when checking whether the application can be submitted?

options.label: Only accepted
accepted and clarification_needed
accepted, forced, and skipped
Anything that is not rejected

explanation.body: A compliance override (forced) and an allowed skip both satisfy completeness. clarification_needed is a soft fail — the participant must accept-anyway or re-upload before submit unblocks.

widgets.title: Where this shape flows
widgets.body: The wizard (Autosave module) holds it in React state and PATCHes deltas; application-service (Lifecycle module) merges those deltas under a row lock; the rule engine evaluates against it; the ownership engine writes the ownership array and its ENG-250 markers.

modules.title: Config → Wizard
modules.summary: Nobody builds these forms by writing JSX. A client's entire application is a static ClientConfig object — fields composed from reusable field-sets, rules, computed values, and a people policy. At render time deriveStages() turns config + current answers into the wizard. The playground below runs the same visibility rules the real derivation uses.

commentary.body: Config + current answers in, wizard out. The loop order comes from stageOrder if the config declares one (this client does: company → questionnaire → owners), else a default category order. Note this function is pure — it runs identically in the browser (per keystroke) and on the server (before submit).

Per category: collect the fields whose category matches, sort by position (the 10/20/30 gaps exist so you can insert between later), and stamp each with a live isVisible() verdict — that call is the rule engine, next module.
One boolean decides whether this category deserves to exist as a stage: does it have at least one visible field right now?
People stages are policy-gated, not field-gated: no collectDirectors → no directors stage, ever — even if director fields exist in the config.
Empty non-people stages are skipped entirely. A stage whose fields were all hidden by rules simply doesn't appear in the wizard — no greyed-out tabs, no placeholder.
Stage names support tokens: this client names its first stage {company_name}, so the tab literally shows the applicant's company.
The result drives the tab strip, the progress ring, and — server-side inside getApplicationState() — the submit validation. One derivation, two runtimes, zero drift.

To add it for every client, add it to the field-set in lib/field-sets/. Configs are registered once at startup and resolved per-org at request time.

widgets.title: Connects forward
widgets.body: The isVisible() call inside deriveStages() is the rule engine — next module. On the client it's memoized by useStageDerivation; on the server the same function runs inside getApplicationState() before submit, so client and server can never disagree about what the form looks like.

modules.title: The Rule Engine
modules.summary: A ~120-line pure JSON-predicate evaluator is the brain of the product: it decides what's visible, what's required, and what still blocks submit — identically in the browser and on the server. The playground below mirrors the real six-case "personal guarantee" decision table. Fill the form like an applicant; watch the logic think.

options.label: Under 3 years
3+ years
Under $5M
$5M or more

inputs.label: Months/year the card balance is paid in full

options.label: 12 Months (All)
Fewer than 12

inputs.label: Credit limit requested > 25% of gross revenue?

explanation.body: Case 1 — time in business < 3 years: operations_start_date within 3 years of today, checked with dateWithinYears against a UTC-midnight cutoff.

Case 2 — computed.adjusted_gross_income < $5,000,000. The arithmetic computed value (gross_revenue_12m × gross_profit_margin × 0.01) runs first and feeds this comparison: an arithmetic computed value feeding a decision table.
Case 3 — the business is not profitable: is_profitable === false.
Case 4 — doesn't pay the balance in full all 12 months: months_pay_in_full exists AND ≠ "12". An unanswered question never satisfies a rule.
Case 5 — a cross-field valueRef comparison: credit_limit_requested > gross_revenue_12m × factor 0.25. Both sides must be numbers or the condition bails false.
Case 6 — debt > 4× net income: total_debt_outstanding > net_income_last_year × factor 4, the second valueRef case in the table.
No case matched → the computed value's default (false) applies. Guarantor fields stay hidden — and cleared — for every person.

widgets.title: Person-scoped fields
widgets.body: Guarantor fields (real estate owned, personal tax return, credit check consent) are person-scoped: their rule is person.is_ubo AND computed.needs_personal_guarantee. When the flag flips they pop in — visible and required — for a UBO, but never for a director-only person. Person-scoped requirement checks loop every active person with a person.* context.

widgets.title: Inside evaluate() — one recursion, the whole language
code: export function evaluate(condition: Condition, ctx: RuleContext): boolean {
if ('and' in condition) return condition.and.every((c) => evaluate(c, ctx));
if ('or' in condition)  return condition.or.some((c) => evaluate(c, ctx));
if (typeof actual !== 'number' || typeof refVal !== 'number') return false;
const target = condition.factor != null ? refVal * condition.factor : refVal;
// ...neq / gt / in / contains / dateWithinYears / isNull / exists...

commentary.body: Trace case 5 of the personal-guarantee table: { ref: "credit_limit_requested", op: "gt", valueRef: "gross_revenue_12m", factor: 0.25 } — with limit $1M and revenue $22M. The ctx is the flattened data: field values at the top level, plus computed.* and (for person fields) person.* namespaces.
Literal escape hatch first. This is how a config hard-hides a field: { field: "legal_entity_type", visible: false } — the condition IS the boolean.

The compound layer is just recursion: and = every, or = some, not = negate. That's the entire boolean algebra of the product — no parser, no DSL strings, just structured JSON all the way down. (Not our case today; case 5 is a leaf.)
resolve("credit_limit_requested", ctx) walks the dotted path → 1,000,000. A missing key resolves to undefined, which every operator treats as falsy — unanswered questions never satisfy a rule.
Case 5 has a valueRef, so we're comparing two fields: resolve gross_revenue_12m → 22,000,000. Both must be numbers (or bail false). Then target = 22,000,000 × 0.25 = 5,500,000.
op: "gt" → is 1,000,000 > 5,500,000? No — case 5 misses, and the decision table moves on to case 6. Push the credit limit past $5.5M in the playground and watch this exact line flip the case green.

Every non-valueRef leaf lands in this switch — equality, ranges, set membership, date windows, existence. ~40 lines encode the entire condition language, which is why the whole engine stays trivially testable and can run on every keystroke.

widgets.title: Why pure functions matter here
widgets.body: The engine has no I/O and no side effects, so the identical code runs on every keystroke in the browser AND inside submitApplication() on the server. The client literally cannot submit something the server would reject — they share one brain. The defaults also matter: a field with no rule is visible and not required, so most fields need no rule at all.

questions.prompt: The applicant picked retail, filled inventory_storage, then switches industry to saas. What actually happens to that stored value?

options.label: The field hides but the value stays in data.fields silently
The field hides AND the client clears the stale value to null, so it never reaches the server
The field stays visible until the next save completes
The server rejects the next PATCH as inconsistent

explanation.body: visibilityAwareUpdateField re-evaluates every field's visibility after each change (with recomputed computed values) and nulls anything that just went invisible — otherwise the stale value could satisfy a requirement or leak into a webhook.

questions.prompt: Predict the engine: operations started 10 years ago, revenue $30M, margin 10%, profitable, pays in full all 12 months, limit $1M, debt $0, net income $2M. Which personal-guarantee case fires?

options.label: Case 1 — time in business
Case 2 — adjusted_gross_income = 30M × 0.10 = $3M, which is < $5M
Case 5 — the credit limit is too high vs revenue
No case fires — needs_personal_guarantee is false

explanation.body: The arithmetic computed value runs first: 30,000,000 × 10 × 0.01 = 3,000,000. Case 1 needs < 3 years (no), case 2 compares computed.adjusted_gross_income < 5,000,000 → true. First match wins; later cases aren't even evaluated.

widgets.title: One more consumer
widgets.body: getMissingRequirements() walks every visible+required field with no value — the invariant being invisible fields never block submission. Its person-scoped sibling loops every active person with a person.* context.

modules.title: Ownership — ENG-250
modules.summary: Nearly every recent PR is ENG-250: find who ultimately owns a company — the UBO — through layers of holding companies, spending as few paid registry credits as possible, and never fabricating data. The engine's load-bearing rule: Phase 1 explores, only Phase 3 prunes. The classic trap that rule exists for is a diamond: an owner who is sub-threshold on every individual path but over the threshold in total.

widgets.title: Three-phase engine trace — explore, cumulate, render

description.body: A credit-bounded, heaviest-first frontier walk. Every shareholder becomes an occurrence — even ones that look hopelessly small on this path — and corporate parents earn a paid registry fetch only through the budget's single charge() chokepoint. Conspicuously absent: any effective-% threshold check.

A pure per-identity summation — diamond aggregation. 9% via one path plus 10% via another is 19%, and at a 15% threshold that's a UBO. Identity is keyed on registration number + country, never display name. One unknown occurrence means the entity can never be proven sub-threshold.

Only now does pruning happen: each identity's cumulative % is compared — unrounded — against the UBO threshold. Sub-threshold owners collapse into the background box; unknown stakes are force-surfaced as "% unknown", never hidden as 0%.

widgets.title: Phase 1 recursion gates — does this shareholder earn a paid fetch?

options.label: Corporate (a holding company)
Individual (a person)

inputs.label: Direct stake known and ≥ the 1% floor?
Already an ancestor on this path (cycle)?
Registry credits left in the budget?

explanation.body: Individuals are leaves: they can be UBOs but they have no registry parents to fetch. The occurrence is still recorded for Phase 2's sum.

rules.outcome: no fetch — sub-floor or unknown stake

explanation.body: An unknown percentage (?? 0) or a direct stake under the 1% floor never earns a paid fetch — the engine refuses to spend a credit on a branch of unknowable weight. But the occurrence was already recorded, so the holder is never silently dropped.
A owns B owns A would loop forever. The ancestor set is per-path on purpose: a diamond revisits the same entity on a different path, and that must be allowed.
Depth 8 is the backstop against pathological chains — the last of the only four recursion gates.
An exhausted budget marks the layer with an explicit "we stopped for budget" marker — distinguishable from a registry that genuinely has no data, so the chart can say so honestly.

defaultOutcome.outcome: fetch the parent record and push to the frontier

explanation.body: The child inherits the multiplied effectivePct so chains keep diluting, plus a copy of pathAncestors. Note there is no effective-% threshold gate anywhere in this table: Phase 1 explores, only Phase 3 prunes.

widgets.title: The code that enforces "explore, don't prune"
code: // stake `undefined` ≠ stated 0%: registry listed a holder with NO %
occurrences.push(occ);   // ALL shareholders stored — even sub-threshold
frontier.push({ record, stableId, effectivePct, depth: node.depth + 1,

commentary.body: We just popped a node off the max-heap — heaviest effective % first, because a tight credit cap should buy the most threshold-revealing fetches.

The ENG-250 subtlety: ownership_percentage == null means the registry listed a holder but stated NO stake. That is not 0%. stakeKnown rides along to Phase 2 (where one unknown occurrence poisons "provably sub-threshold") and Phase 3 (force-surface as "% unknown").

Chain-multiply: a 60% owner of a node worth 20% of the root is worth 20 × 60 / 100 = 12%. Identity is keyed on registration number + country, never display name — two registries may spell the same holding company differently.

EVERY shareholder becomes an occurrence — including ones that look hopelessly small on this path. Phase 2 may promote them: 9% here plus 10% on another path is 19%, and at a 15% threshold that's a UBO. Prune here and diamonds lose their owners.

The only four recursion gates: individuals are leaves; a direct stake under the 1% floor (or unknown — ?? 0) doesn't earn a paid fetch; a per-path ancestor set kills cycles (A owns B owns A); depth 8 is the backstop. Conspicuously absent: any effective-% threshold check. Phase 1 explores; only Phase 3 prunes.

The fetch is the money moment — credit-gated through the budget's single charge() chokepoint and memoised per run (a diamond parent reached via two children is fetched once, rendered twice). An exhausted budget marks the layer credit_truncated — an explicit "we stopped for budget" marker, distinguishable from a registry that genuinely has no data.

Recurse: the child inherits the multiplied effectivePct so chains keep diluting, and a COPY of pathAncestors — the cycle guard is per-path on purpose, because a diamond revisits the same entity on a different path and that must be allowed.

widgets.title: The bug class this design kills
widgets.body: An unknown stake (ownership_percentage == null) is NOT 0%. It's recorded as an occurrence (the owner is never silently dropped) but not recursed into (don't burn a credit on a branch of unknowable weight), and in Phase 2 one unknown occurrence means the entity can never be proven sub-threshold — so Phase 3 force-surfaces it with "% unknown" instead of hiding it in the background box.

// legacy all_owners_added attestation when no wizard meta exists.

caption.body: Two more pieces close the loop. Analysts can replay the whole engine against cached registry data — explainOwnershipFromCache() uses an Infinity cap with a non-persisting ledger, so "why isn't owner X on the chart?" costs zero credits. And submission is gated by this one shared helper, used by both the wizard UI and the submit endpoint so they can never disagree.

questions.prompt: If Phase 1 pruned every branch whose per-path effective % was below the threshold, what would break?

options.label: Nothing — it would just run faster and spend fewer credits
Cycle detection would loop forever
Diamond aggregation — an owner who is sub-threshold on every individual path but ≥ threshold in total would never be summed, so real UBOs vanish
The credit budget would be overspent

explanation.body: That's the load-bearing rule: Phase 1 explores, only Phase 3 prunes. Recursion is gated by credits, a tiny direct-% floor, and a per-path cycle guard — never by effective %. Only Phase 2's cumulative sum may be compared to the threshold.

questions.prompt: The registry lists a corporate shareholder but states no percentage. The engine…

options.label: Treats it as 0% and collapses it into the background box
Records the occurrence, does NOT recurse into it, and force-surfaces it as "% unknown" — never as 0%
Estimates the stake from the remaining unallocated percentage
Aborts enrichment for the whole application

explanation.body: Unknown ≠ zero. The holder is never silently dropped (occurrence recorded, force-surfaced), but the engine won't burn a paid credit exploring a branch whose weight it can't even see — and one unknown occurrence means the entity can never be "proven" sub-threshold.

modules.title: Lifecycle & the Backend Spine
modules.summary: lib/application-service.ts (~2,800 lines) is the spine: every create, update, upload, submit, and decision passes through it. Two things to internalize: the status lifecycle below, and the one pattern all fifteen service functions share.

description.body: Writable — the row exists (createApplication) but no invite email was sent (sendInvite: false). The config version is frozen onto the row at this moment.
Writable — the invite email went out with the link_slug URL. Registry enrichment is already running fire-and-forget in the background.
Writable — flipped automatically by the FIRST participant PATCH. This is where applications live most of their life.
submitApplication re-ran the full getApplicationState() validation server-side inside the row lock, found nothing missing, and froze the data. Webhooks + Slack fire after commit.
An analyst is looking at it in the dashboard. approve/reject are accepted from either submitted or review.
Terminal — approveApplication guards the transition (only from submitted/review), stamps completed_at, then notifies fire-and-forget.
Terminal — mirror of approve. A rejected application also refuses to mint new participant JWTs.

commentary.body: Data PATCHes are only accepted in created, sent, and in_progress — isWritableStatus() guards every mutation. Once submitted, the data is frozen for review.

widgets.title: The one pattern: lock → guard → merge → recompute → commit → notify
code: export async function participantUpdateApplicationData(id, patch, participantId, scopedPersonId?) {
const row = await lockApplicationForUpdate(tx, id);   // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
if (!row) return { success: false, error: 'Application not found' };
return { success: false, error: `Cannot update application in ${row.status} status` };
return { success: false, error: 'Collaborators can only update their assigned person' };
if (!validation.valid) return { success: false, error: validation.errors.join('; ') };
.set({ data: merged, computed_cache: computed, status: newStatus, updated_at: new Date() })
// activity log rows written OUTSIDE the transaction — non-critical path

commentary.body: Lock. Everything happens inside one transaction that starts with SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Two participants (or a participant plus a background enrichment job) hitting the same row are serialized — the second waits, then reads the already-updated state. No lost updates on the JSONB blob, ever.
Guard. Writes are only legal in created / sent / in_progress. A PATCH against a submitted application gets an explicit error, not a silent drop — you saw this state machine above.
Scope. A collaborator's JWT carries a personId; they may only touch their assigned person. Any attempt to patch fields, ownership, or entities is refused outright.

Merge, deny-by-default. A naive spread would let a buggy client blank out documents, consent, or registry rows. mergeParticipantPatch lets the patch touch participant-owned data only; everything server-owned is re-applied from the locked row.

Audit. Diffing before/after catches registry rows soft-deleted in this patch — each dismissed person or ownership edge gets its own activity-log entry, because a regulator will one day ask why a registry-supplied owner disappeared.

Recompute + commit. Computed values are refreshed into computed_cache (so dashboards can filter without re-running the engine), the first-ever write flips created/sent → in_progress, and the transaction commits atomically.

Notify, outside. Activity logging — and in the submit/approve siblings, webhooks and Slack — happens AFTER commit, fire-and-forget. Slow or broken downstreams can't roll back a user's save. Every one of the ~15 service functions follows this exact shape.

widgets.title: Why SELECT … FOR UPDATE?
widgets.body: Two participants — or a participant plus a background enrichment job — can hit the same application at once. The row lock serializes them so the JSONB blob never suffers a lost-update race. Slow work (webhooks, Slack, enrichment) always happens after commit, fire-and-forget, so a broken customer endpoint can never roll back a submit.

widgets.title: Deny-by-default merge
widgets.body: A naive { ...current, ...patch } would let a buggy client blank out documents, consent, or registry ownership. mergeParticipantPatch only lets participants touch participant-owned data; everything server-owned is re-applied from the locked row. Dismissed registry rows are detected by diffing before/after — each gets its own audit-log entry, because regulators care WHY a registry-supplied owner disappeared.

questions.prompt: A PATCH arrives for an application whose status is submitted. The service layer…

options.label: Merges it and leaves the status untouched
Queues it until an analyst moves the app back to review
Rejects it — isWritableStatus() only allows created / sent / in_progress
Returns 404 to hide the application's existence

explanation.body: Every mutation locks the row and guards the status first. Once submitted, the data is frozen for review — the participant gets an explicit "Cannot update application in submitted status" error.

modules.title: Autosave & the Wizard
modules.summary: The wizard is React Context + hooks — no Redux. The core loop: a keystroke updates state instantly, stages into a pendingChanges ref, and a 2-second debounce collapses a burst of typing into exactly one PATCH.

widgets.title: The autosave loop — the full journey of a keystroke

description.body: State updates instantly — the input never lags — and the delta stages into the pendingChanges ref, keyed by field id.
Every keystroke RESETS the 2-second timer — the PATCH fires 2s after you stop, not 2s after you start. A burst of typing collapses into exactly one request.
The accumulated delta is captured and the ref immediately reset, so keystrokes landing while the PATCH is in flight accumulate separately — nothing lost, nothing double-sent.
The delta — not the whole document — lands in participantUpdateApplicationData, which locks the row and merges deny-by-default.
Success flips the badge to Saved and clears the localStorage backup. Failure restores the delta to pendingChanges for retry and writes a backup — with national_insurance_number deliberately stripped.

widgets.title: flushSave() and its wrapper, stepped through
code: if (safeData.fields) { const f = { ...safeData.fields }; delete f.national_insurance_number; safeData.fields = f; }

commentary.body: The debounce fired (or saveNow() forced it — submit does this and aborts if the save fails, so the server never validates stale state). First: disarm any still-pending timer.

Capture the accumulated delta and immediately reset the ref. This is the subtle bit: keystrokes that land while the PATCH is in flight accumulate into a fresh empty object — nothing is lost, nothing is double-sent.

PATCH the delta, not the whole document. The server (the Lifecycle module's walkthrough) locks the row and merges deny-by-default — so even a malicious hand-crafted patch can't blank server-owned data.
Failure path 1 — retry. The failed delta is merged back UNDER whatever accumulated during the flight (newer edits win), so the next debounce cycle retries everything.

Failure path 2 — the safety net. A localStorage backup is written in case the tab dies before a retry succeeds… with national_insurance_number deliberately deleted first. Sensitive data never rests in browser storage.

Success. The badge flips to "Saved", the backup is cleared. When the SERVER later changes data the client didn't author (doc extraction, enrichment), refresh() runs: flush my edits → GET → re-queue anything that raced in.

widgets.title: Why clear hidden fields?
widgets.body: Pick "retail", fill inventory_storage, then switch industry to "SaaS" — that field is now invisible but its value still sits in data.fields. Left there it would be PATCHed to the server, could wrongly satisfy a requirement, and could leak into a webhook. So visibilityAwareUpdateField re-evaluates visibility after every change and nulls anything that just went dark — the data always matches what the rule engine says should exist.

questions.prompt: An applicant types 12 characters over ~3 seconds, then stops. How many PATCH requests fire?

options.label: Twelve — one per keystroke
Exactly one, about 2 seconds after the last keystroke
Two — one per 2-second window
Zero until the field loses focus

explanation.body: Each keystroke resets the 2s debounce timer, so a burst collapses into a single PATCH containing the accumulated pendingChanges delta.

widgets.title: Server round-trip
widgets.body: The PATCH lands in the Lifecycle module's participantUpdateApplicationData. When the server changes data the client didn't author (document auto-extraction, enrichment), the wizard calls refresh(): flush my edits first, then GET, then re-queue anything that raced in.

modules.title: Document Validation
modules.summary: When a participant uploads a passport or bank statement, an AI assembly line decides its fate and streams progress over SSE: OCR → classify → clarity → adequacy → date rules → verdict. Deterministic code brackets the LLM — extracted key-value pairs backstop extraction, and date arithmetic is never left to a model.

description.body: Text and key-value pairs are extracted first. Under 50 characters extracted trips isLowText — the hinge that smart-switches the provider so a vision model reads the scanned image instead of trusting OCR text.
An LLM names the documentType with a confidence score. documentType "unknown" is a hard stop at the verdict.
Is the image readable? Critical severity that is not acceptable fails the document outright — the participant must re-upload (the state machine loops back to pending).

Does the document actually cover what the field needs — required fields present, and the name matching the person it's attached to? adequacy.nameMatch === false is an automatic fail regardless of confidence.
Date arithmetic is never left to a model: deterministic code checks expiry and recency windows — a bank statement from 5 months ago fails a "within 3 months" requirement in plain code.
determineValidationStatus() folds it all: hard stops → FAILED, soft doubts → NEEDS_REVIEW, otherwise PASSED. Progress streamed to the wizard's card over SSE at 10% / 50% / 75% / 90%.

code: export function determineValidationStatus(classification, clarity, adequacy, overallConfidence, itemType?, acceptableDocTypes?): ValidationStatus {
adequacy.nameMatch === false ||          // name mismatch = automatic fail

caption.body: The verdict function, verbatim. PASSED → document status accepted · NEEDS_REVIEW → clarification_needed · FAILED → rejected — the state machine from the Data Model module. After acceptance, extracted identity fields (name, DOB, address) auto-populate the person record, but only for fields whose config opted in via automation.source = 'document_extraction' — which is why the wizard calls refresh() afterwards.

widgets.title: Observability is not optional
widgets.body: Every classification/clarity/adequacy call is wrapped in traceAIOperation() (Braintrust/OTel) and analytics tracing with privacyMode: true so document contents never leak into analytics. If you add an LLM call anywhere in the codebase, it must be traced — that's a standing repo rule.

questions.prompt: A passport is crisp, classification confidence is 0.98… but the name doesn't match the person it's attached to. Verdict?

options.label: PASSED — confidence dominates
NEEDS_REVIEW — a human should decide
FAILED — adequacy.nameMatch === false is a hard stop, regardless of confidence
Depends on which AI provider ran the check

explanation.body: The FAILED block in determineValidationStatus() checks name mismatch before any soft signals. A perfect passport belonging to the wrong person is exactly the fraud case the pipeline exists to catch.

modules.title: Auth & Plumbing
modules.summary: Three kinds of caller, three auth methods — trace each lane hop by hop. Underneath: one Drizzle client over all schemas, QStash-queued webhooks, and subdomain routing for the admin backoffice.

nodes.label: Analyst · login
nodes.description: The analyst lane starts at the org dashboard: login with email or Google.

nodes.label: Participant · link_slug
nodes.description: The participant lane starts from the shareable link: it carries a public link_slug; the secret access_token lives only in the DB.

nodes.label: JWT · 1h · auto-refresh
nodes.description: Verifying your email mints a 1-hour JWT — and minting re-validates the entire chain (participant not blocked, application not expired/rejected, org active), so a JWT can never be issued for a dead application.

nodes.label: personId scope
nodes.description: Collaborator JWTs carry a personId that scopes them to a single person's data.

nodes.label: Partner · bearer key
nodes.description: The partner-system lane authenticates with a bearer API key of the form {clientId}.{secret}.

widgets.title: The two-token model
widgets.body: The shareable link carries a public link_slug; the secret access_token lives only in the DB. Verifying your email mints a 1-hour JWT — and minting re-validates the entire chain (participant not blocked, application not expired/rejected, org active), so a JWT can never be issued for a dead application.

code: const payload = { id: `evt_${crypto.randomUUID()}`, type: eventType, timestamp: ..., organizationId, applicationId, data };
const [delivery] = await db.insert(webhookDeliveryLog).values({ endpoint_id: ep.id, payload }).returning(...);
await qstash.publishJSON({ url: `${getAppUrl()}/api/webhooks/deliver`, body: { deliveryId: delivery.id }, retries: MAX_WEBHOOK_ATTEMPTS - 1 });

caption.body: Outbound: webhooks that can't hurt you. emitWebhook() never POSTs synchronously — it writes a delivery row and hands the job to QStash, which calls back with retries. Deliveries are HMAC-SHA256 signed; repeated failures warn the org, then auto-disable the endpoint. A slow customer server can never block a submit.

widgets.title: Three facts that save you a debugging afternoon
widgets.body: 1) Fields marked sensitive: true (like national_insurance_number) are stripped from webhook payloads and from localStorage backups. 2) Feature flags are server-only and authoritative — the registry-provider flags decide per-org registry spend (and its cap) from a dashboard, no deploy; never call a flag from a client component. 3) admin.localhost does not work in dev — browsers don't share cookies across localhost subdomains. Use a tunnel or hit /backoffice directly.

widgets.title: Logging convention
widgets.body: Inside request scope, prefer the request logger (getRequestLogger()) over console.* — but service-layer catch handlers stick with console.* because they also fire from cron/queue paths where getRequestLogger() throws.

widget.title: You've driven the whole system — where to go next
widget.body: The shape, config → form, the rule engine, the ownership engine the team is actively building, the transactional spine, the live wizard, the AI pipeline, and the doors in and out. Next: run the dev server and fill a seeded application with the network tab open; then read the last ~15 PRs — they're almost all ENG-250, and now they'll read fluently. Checkpoints missed? They reset per-browser — reload and retry.
